conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m honored to meet you. My role is to support new mothers as they navigate the emotional ups and downs that can arrive after a baby is born.

In a moment I’ll share a brief questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a way for us to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. Your answers stay completely confidential between you and our care team, and there are no right or wrong responses—just whatever feels true for you.

We’ll go through ten questions together. I’ll ask each one conversationally, and you can answer in whatever way feels most comfortable. If anything feels difficult or confusing, we can pause and talk it through.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, when you think about the times you were able to laugh or see the funny side of things, how often did that happen for you?

I guess I can still laugh sometimes… but it’s pretty rare. Mostly I just feel kind of flat, like things that used to be funny don’t really reach me anymore. Maybe once or twice this week I chuckled at something on my phone, but it didn’t feel the same—more like I was going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not very much… I mean, I can still laugh a little, but it feels forced most of the time. Maybe once or twice this week I sort of smiled at something, but it fades fast and I go right back to feeling heavy.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Honestly… not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately it’s like nothing feels worth looking forward to. I still go through the motions, hoping I’ll feel something, but it’s pretty flat. Maybe once this week I thought, “It might be nice to sit outside,” but the spark lasted about two seconds before the sad feeling came back.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not reading his cues or I’m a lousy mom. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and I sat there crying, telling myself I was wasting the one thing I’m supposed to be able to give him. Most days there’s at least one moment where I’m convinced I’m failing him somehow, even when my head sort of knows that’s not fair.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… pretty much every day. My heart races over things that don’t even make sense—like I’ll stare at the baby monitor convinced he’s stopped breathing, or I’ll lie in bed rehearsing all the ways something terrible could happen on a simple walk to the mailbox. There’s this constant knot in my stomach even when everything looks fine on the outside. I know it’s “for no good reason,” but knowing doesn’t make the worry shut off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah, a few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s going on. The other night I was just warming up a bottle and out of nowhere my heart started racing and I had to grip the counter to steady myself. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and on edge for the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most of the time it feels like that. It’s like every small task—folding a basket of laundry, answering one text—turns into this giant mountain. I’ll look around the living room and see bottles and burp cloths everywhere and just freeze, thinking, “I can’t do all of this.” I still push through for the baby, but I feel overwhelmed more often than I feel okay.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… pretty much every night this week. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—replaying everything I think I did wrong, worrying about the baby, feeling guilty that I’m not happier. It takes me at least an hour to fall asleep, and when I do I jerk awake a couple of times in a panic. I’m lucky if I get four broken hours before he’s up again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes… that’s been most days. It’s like this gray cloud sitting on me. I wake up already feeling down, and even when I try to do something “nice” for myself—like take a shower or watch a show—the sadness just lingers. I’ll tear up out of nowhere, and some afternoons I end up crying while I’m rocking the baby, hoping he can’t sense how unhappy I feel.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Yesterday I just sat in the nursery with the lights off and cried while he napped—nothing specific set me off, just this heavy sadness that wouldn’t lift. It’s not all-day sobbing, but when it hits, the tears come fast and I feel like I can’t stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…It’s crossed my mind, yeah. Just fleeting things—like when I’m really overwhelmed I’ll think, “What if I just disappeared?”—but I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to leave my baby. They’re more like scary flashes I try to push away. Still, the fact that they show up at all frightens me.

You've shared how the joy and sparkle that used to come easily now feel distant and heavy. Over the past week laughter has been rare and forced, the simplest tasks feel like mountains, and a constant knot of worry sits in your stomach. You described crying alone in the nursery, gripping the counter through sudden panic, and lying awake replaying every perceived parenting mistake. Even though part of you knows these thoughts are unfair, the sadness, guilt, and intrusive flashes of disappearing keep returning.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports markedly reduced ability to laugh, describing it as mostly forced and fleeting, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory joy, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient clearly endorses self-blame "a lot" and "most days," aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, pervasive anxiety with physical symptoms and intrusive catastrophic thoughts, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic-attack episodes occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports being overwhelmed "most of the time," unable to manage routine tasks, matching "Yes, most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to unhappiness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Response describes pervasive daily sadness, frequent crying, and inability to feel better—aligns with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Response confirms crying "a couple of times this week" and describes sudden, difficult-to-stop tears, aligning with "Yes, quite often".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring intrusive thoughts of disappearing when overwhelmed, which maps to "Sometimes" (score 2).</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score ≥14 indicates probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>; with 26/30, responses align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood and loss of interest most days, plus marked anxiety, guilt, insomnia, panic symptoms, and passive suicidal ideation causing functional impairment. Item 10 score of 2 warrants immediate safety review. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or local perinatal mental-health team
2. Request evaluation for both <med>antidepressant medication</med> and evidence-based therapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>
3. Develop a written safety plan including 24-h support numbers and removal of potential means of self-harm
4. Encourage 15-20 min of morning daylight and acceptance of practical help with housework or night feeds to improve <sym>sleep</sym> and reduce <sym>fatigue</sym>
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS within one week to monitor score trend
6. Inform trusted family/friends of warning signs so they can activate help quickly
7. Call 988 (US) or your local emergency services if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe at any moment
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  

Identified symptoms / behavioral indicators:  
- Persistent low mood, frequent tearfulness, minimal reactivity to pleasant events  
- Marked anhedonia (“nothing feels worth looking forward to”)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt regarding parenting performance  
- Daily, distressing anxiety and panic episodes without clear trigger  
- Overwhelm and task paralysis; difficulty coping with routine infant care demands  
- Sleep initiation / maintenance problems directly linked to ruminative worry and low mood  
- Passive, transient self-harm ideation (no plan, intent, or desire to die)  

Pattern: Symptoms present most days over the past week, causing functional impairment and emotional distress; no evidence of psychosis or manic features.  

Risk factors:  
- Postpartum period (infant <12 mo)  
- Prior sleep deprivation secondary to infant care  
- Lack of perceived social / practical support  
- Self-harm ideation (safety flag)  

Screening observation:  
Responses are consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; passive suicidal ideation present. Recommend immediate safety assessment and expedited referral to perinatal mental-health specialist for evaluation of diagnosis and level of care.
